title: PLC, IP3, DAG and Protein Kinase C

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Phospholipase C hydrolyzes the bond between {{c1::glycerol}} and the linking phosphate of PIP2.
cards.quote: Phospholipase C (PLC) hydrolyzes the bond between glycerol and the linking phosphate.

cards.front: When phospholipase C cuts PIP2, which two products form, and where does each end up?
cards.back: IP3 leaves into the cytosol; DAG stays in the membrane.
cards.why: The phosphate leaves with the inositol ring, so a lipid named for two phosphates yields a soluble product named for three.
cards.quote: so a lipid named for two phosphates yields a soluble product named for three

cards.front: Each product of the PLC cut is a {{c1::second messenger}}, a small molecule made inside a cell in response to an external signal.
cards.quote: Each product is a second messenger, a small molecule made inside a cell in response to an external signal.

cards.front: Why does DAG stay in the membrane after the PLC cut while IP3 leaves?
cards.back: DAG keeps the two fatty acid tails on its glycerol backbone, which sit in the membrane. IP3 is the soluble inositol head group with three phosphates.
cards.quote: Two fatty acid tails on a glycerol backbone sit in the membrane.

cards.front: How does a Gq-coupled receptor switch on PLC-beta?
cards.back: The receptor loads GTP onto Gq alpha, and Gq-GTP activates PLC-beta at the membrane.
cards.quote: A receptor coupled to Gq loads GTP onto Gq alpha, as in GTPase switches, and Gq-GTP activates PLC-beta at the membrane.
cards.section: Two receptor routes converge on the cut

cards.front: What do the SH2 domains of PLC-gamma do, and why can PLC-beta not be switched on this way?
cards.back: SH2 domains recognize phosphorylated tyrosines, so PLC-gamma can dock on an activated receptor tyrosine kinase. PLC-beta is regulated by G proteins, not by receptor phosphotyrosines.
cards.quote: PLC-gamma carries two SH2 domains, which recognize phosphorylated tyrosines in particular sequence contexts, and an SH3 domain, which binds proline-rich protein segments.
cards.section: Two receptor routes converge on the cut

cards.front: A mutant PLC-gamma lacks the tyrosines that a receptor tyrosine kinase phosphorylates but keeps its SH2 domains. The growth factor is added. What happens to docking and to PIP2 cutting?
cards.back: It still docks on the receptor but cuts little PIP2. Docking alone is not activation: the brake on the catalytic barrel stays on until the tyrosines are phosphorylated.
cards.quote: Docking alone is not activation: a PLC-gamma lacking the tyrosines the receptor kinase phosphorylates would still dock but cut little PIP2, because the brake on its catalytic barrel stays on.
cards.section: Two receptor routes converge on the cut

cards.front: How does PLC-beta help end its own activation by Gq?
cards.back: PLC-beta accelerates GTP hydrolysis by Gq. Cutting then continues only while receptors keep reloading Gq with GTP.
cards.quote: PLC-beta accelerates GTP hydrolysis by Gq, helping reset its own activator; cutting continues only while receptors reload Gq.
cards.section: Two receptor routes converge on the cut

cards.front: Which PLC family can acetylcholine at a Gq-coupled muscarinic receptor use, and which can PDGF at its receptor tyrosine kinase use?
cards.back: Acetylcholine: PLC-beta. PDGF: PLC-gamma.
cards.quote: Thus acetylcholine at a Gq-coupled muscarinic receptor can use PLC-beta, and PDGF at its receptor tyrosine kinase can use PLC-gamma.
cards.section: Two receptor routes converge on the cut

cards.front: In the 1983 test of IP3, pancreatic acinar cells were permeabilized before IP3 was added. Why not add IP3 to intact cells?
cards.back: IP3 is too charged to cross an intact plasma membrane, so the cells had to be opened. Internal compartments stayed sealed.
cards.quote: IP3 is too charged to cross an intact membrane, which is why the cells had to be opened.
cards.section: How IP3 earned the name messenger

cards.front: Permeabilized cells are given ATP so that their internal stores take up calcium. Adding IP3 raises free calcium in the medium. Blocking mitochondrial calcium uptake first does not change the rise, but an inhibitor of the ER calcium pump abolishes it. What do these data show?
cards.back: IP3 releases calcium from the ER, not from mitochondria. The rise survives the mitochondrial block but needs an ER store that the pump has filled.
cards.quote: Streb permeabilized pancreatic acinar cells in Irene Schulz's laboratory, making the plasma membrane admit small molecules while internal compartments stayed sealed.
cards.section: How IP3 earned the name messenger

cards.front: The ER holds free calcium at a thousand times or more the resting cytosolic level of about {{c1::100 nM}}.
cards.quote: holds free calcium at a thousand times or more the resting cytosolic level of about 100 nM.
cards.section: How IP3 earned the name messenger

cards.front: Why was the finding that IP3 appears within seconds of hormone arrival not enough to show that IP3 releases calcium?
cards.back: It is only a correlation. A hormone starts many events, so IP3 and calcium could both follow a third cause. The permeabilized-cell test added IP3 directly.
cards.quote: a hormone starts many events, so IP3 and calcium could both follow a third cause.
cards.section: How IP3 earned the name messenger

cards.front: How does the pseudosubstrate keep protein kinase C off?
cards.back: It resembles a substrate but has alanine where the target serine or threonine would be, so it occupies the active site and blocks it.
cards.quote: Its pseudosubstrate resembles a substrate but has alanine where the target serine or threonine would be, so it occupies the active site and blocks it.

cards.front: What does the calcium-loaded C2 domain of conventional PKC bind?
cards.back: Anionic membrane lipids such as phosphatidylserine. This is how calcium targets the kinase to the membrane.
cards.quote: The calcium-loaded C2 domain binds anionic membrane lipids such as phosphatidylserine

cards.front: Assays with purified PKC and defined lipids showed that DAG explained the extra activity of impure lipid preparations. What did DAG change about the kinase's calcium requirement?
cards.back: DAG lets the kinase work at much lower calcium.
cards.quote: traced the extra activity of impure lipid preparations to DAG, which lets the kinase work at much lower calcium.

cards.front: A purified conventional PKC reads 2 units with no additions, 8 with calcium alone, 5 with DAG alone and 66 with both. What would simple addition predict with both, and what does 66 imply?
cards.back: Calcium adds 6 above baseline and DAG adds 3, so addition predicts 2 + 6 + 3 = 11. The measured 66 is 6 times that, so the inputs act synergistically.
cards.quote: A value of 40 is about sevenfold above that expectation, evidence that the inputs act synergistically under these assay conditions.

cards.front: In the model where binding energies add, the C1 contact alone favors the membrane 20-fold and the C2 contact alone 15-fold, acting independently. What is the combined membrane preference?
cards.back: Energies add, so preferences multiply: 20 × 15 = 300-fold.
cards.why: Rests on the rule ΔG(both) ≈ ΔG(C1) + ΔG(C2).
cards.quote: If each contact alone favors the membrane thirtyfold, say, the pair favors it about 30 × 30 = 900-fold.

cards.front: Why is it useful for conventional PKC to need both calcium and DAG rather than either alone?
cards.back: Calcium also rises when voltage-gated channels open, and other lipid reactions make DAG. Needing both means it responds mainly where PLC has just cut PIP2.
cards.quote: so a kinase that answered either input alone would fire for many unrelated reasons.

cards.front: Cytosolic calcium is clamped at its resting level and a Gq-coupled receptor is stimulated, so DAG forms normally. Which PKC class is most likely to be activated: conventional or novel?
cards.back: Novel. Novel PKCs carry DAG-binding C1 domains and a C2-like domain that does not bind calcium, so DAG alone suffices. Conventional PKC also needs calcium for its C2 domain.
cards.quote: conventional and novel PKCs carry two DAG-binding C1 domains, C1A and C1B.

cards.front: Which PKC class does not require DAG or calcium?
cards.back: Atypical PKCs (zeta, iota). Their C1-like domain does not bind DAG.
cards.quote: Not every PKC asks for both signals.

cards.front: In 1982 a phorbol ester was added to PKC assays in place of DAG. What did the result show?
cards.back: A phorbol ester can substitute for DAG and activate PKC directly. Later work showed that it binds the same C1 site.
cards.quote: In 1982 Monique Castagna and Nishizuka's group showed that a phorbol ester can substitute for DAG and activate PKC directly
cards.section: A DAG mimic shows why duration matters

cards.front: Cells are held in a phorbol ester for 24 hours. Compared with a brief Gq stimulus, what happens to the total PKC and to substrate phosphorylation, and why?
cards.back: PKC protein falls and substrate phosphorylation can end up lower. Cells clear DAG quickly but cannot efficiently break down a phorbol ester, and PKC held on for hours is degraded.
cards.quote: A long exposure therefore ends with less enzyme than the cell started with, so a brief signal and a prolonged one can have opposite outcomes.
cards.section: A DAG mimic shows why duration matters

cards.front: Of 46 PKC mutations from human tumors tested in cells, 28 reduce or abolish kinase function and none increases it. What fraction was loss-of-function, and what does that suggest about normal PKC?
cards.back: 28/46 is about 61 percent. Most tumor mutations disable the enzyme, so the working enzyme behaves more like a brake on tumors, at least for the isozymes tested.
cards.quote: Alexandra Newton's laboratory tested 46 PKC mutations from human tumors: most disabled the kinase and none activated it.
cards.section: A DAG mimic shows why duration matters

cards.front: Does the loss-of-function pattern in tumor PKC mutations mean every PKC isozyme restrains tumors?
cards.back: No. The direction depends on isozyme and context. PKC-iota in lung cancer can act as an oncogene.
cards.quote: although the direction depends on isozyme and context; PKC-iota in lung cancer can act as an oncogene.
cards.section: A DAG mimic shows why duration matters

cards.front: How are IP3 and DAG removed after the signal?
cards.back: Phosphatases dephosphorylate IP3, or a kinase adds a fourth phosphate. DAG kinase converts DAG to phosphatidic acid.
cards.quote: Phosphatases dephosphorylate IP3, or a kinase adds a fourth phosphate. DAG kinase converts DAG to phosphatidic acid.

cards.front: IP3 breakdown is blocked but DAG kinase stays active. Which messenger outlasts the other, and why does conventional PKC output still fall?
cards.back: IP3 outlasts DAG. PKC output falls as DAG becomes phosphatidic acid, because calcium targeting without the DAG contact is a weaker input. Calcium may still decline as the ER store runs down and pumps remove it.
cards.quote: Conventional PKC output can fall either way as DAG is converted to phosphatidic acid, because calcium targeting without the DAG contact is a weaker input.

cards.front: A designed kinase has a pseudosubstrate-blocked kinase domain, a C1 domain for DAG, and a domain that binds a small G protein only in its GTP form. DAG is high and the G protein holds GDP. What is the output, and which rule does it rest on?
cards.back: Weak output. Each contact alone gives only brief membrane visits, so DAG alone should not strongly activate it. This is the coincidence-detector rule: strong output needs both contacts.
cards.quote: DAG alone should not strongly activate the detector while Ras holds GDP.

cards.front: Why would a kinase that either of two signals could switch fully on be a poor detector of two overlapping events?
cards.back: It would be an OR gate, whose output cannot tell the pair of events from a single one.
cards.quote: if either could switch the kinase on fully, you would have built an OR gate

cards.front: Why does cutting the tether between the PKC pseudosubstrate and the kinase domain produce activity?
cards.back: The pseudosubstrate no longer blocks the active site, so the kinase no longer needs the normal signal. A caspase does this to PKC-delta in programmed cell death.
cards.quote: Cutting the tether between a PKC pseudosubstrate and kinase domain creates activity that no longer needs the normal signal

cards.front: PDGF stimulates PLC-gamma in a cell whose IP3 receptors are missing. Which messenger forms, and how do conventional and novel PKC respond?
cards.back: The PIP2 cut still makes both IP3 and DAG, but with no IP3 receptors there is no IP3-driven calcium rise. Novel PKC, needing only DAG, can still be activated. Conventional PKC gets a weaker input without calcium targeting.
cards.quote: Calcium and DAG appear together at the inner face of the plasma membrane mainly when PLC has just cut PIP2 there.

cards.front: IP3 opens a calcium channel. Does IP3 carry calcium into the cytosol?
cards.back: No. IP3 opens the calcium channel on the ER. The channel carries the calcium.
cards.quote: IP3 opens a calcium channel; it does not carry calcium.

cards.front: Besides Gq, which G protein subunits can activate some PLC-beta forms?
cards.back: Beta-gamma subunits released from G proteins such as Gi, especially for PLC-beta2 and PLC-beta3.
cards.quote: Some forms, especially PLC-beta2 and PLC-beta3, also respond to beta-gamma subunits released from G proteins such as Gi.
cards.section: Two receptor routes converge on the cut
